title: Count Every Valid Route (Backtracking)
real_world_story: A patrol robot must choose a route to the dock that never revisits a cell, because a guarded corridor locks behind it. The controller wants to compare how many such routes exist before picking the safest one.

real_world_connection.input_represents: Floor grid where 0 is open and 1 is blocked, plus the start and dock cells
real_world_connection.query_represents: The start cell and the dock cell
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Walking a route cell by cell and undoing each step to try the next direction

problem_statement: Given a tiny R x C floor grid of 0 (open) and 1 (blocked), a start cell (sr, sc) and a dock cell (dr, dc), count every route from start to dock that visits no cell twice, moving 4-directionally. Every backtracking walk that reaches the dock and never revisits a cell is one valid route.
task: Return the number of different valid routes from start to dock. When the start and the dock are the same free cell, the empty route already counts as one.
input_format: The first line contains two integers R and C. The next R lines each contain C integers (0 or 1). The final line contains four integers sr sc dr dc.
output_format: Print the number of different valid routes from start to dock. Print 0 when no valid route exists.

examples.explanation: From (0,0) to (1,1) there are two valid routes: right then down, and down then right.

expected_algorithm.name: Backtracking
expected_algorithm.reason: Each route is built one cell at a time with a visited mark that is added and removed, so every exhaustive walk explores exactly the set of simple routes and each one is counted once.

complexity.time: Exponential in the worst case, but tiny boards keep the count tractable
complexity.space: O(R * C) for the visited marks and the recursion depth

hint: Move to one of the four neighbours, mark the cell visited, then recurse.
When the dock is reached, count one route and return.
Unmark the cell before trying the next direction so other routes can use it again.
real_world_takeaway: Backtracking enumerates every feasible option, which is exactly what an auditor needs before it can certify the safest patrol route.
